doc.title: Kristen Korb interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 16, 2000

title: Discovering jazz in Boise and the junior high jazz camp
summary: Born in Montana, raised partly in Boise; a school choir sparks her love of jazz, she takes up bass and attends a high school jazz camp as a seventh grader.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Well I was born and raised in Montana, the jazz mecca of the west. And actually my family had moved to Boise, Idaho where my father had a western wear store. And that was like through my kindergarten and junior high years. And when I was in sixth grade the junior high choir and band programs came through the schools and I was sitting on the gym floor with all the other kids and I heard the choir sing “Save the Bones for Henry Jones/’Cause Henry Don’t Eat No Meat,” and I don’t know why but it just knocked me out. I was just like oh this is the coolest thing. Because up until that point all I knew was country & western music. I thought was going to be Barbara Mandrell. I loved playing guitar, I did Anne Murray songs, and we did a little bluegrass in the family, my younger brothers played and so we all kind of would play that stuff. But when I got into junior high I wanted to play for that vocal jazz group. And the choir director said well it’s a bass guitar, but if you want to come in on your lunch hours or before school or after school, you’re more than welcome to play the instrument and see what you think. Well it didn’t take very long for me to get into that. And he encouraged me to go to a jazz camp that summer after my seventh grade year. Except for it was a high school camp. He said, “You know this is very serious. If you’re going to go to this camp, you’ve got to practice. Because if they find out you are in seventh grade, they’re going to ship you home faster than anything.” So they had to start pulling me out of the practice rooms at this camp because I was so afraid that they were going to send me home, that I wouldn’t be good enough, that I was just practicing everything. So I did my first vocal solo there, “I’ve Got

a Crush on You,” and I was so scared, it was [sings]. But the camp was so cool because it was like this big, warm fuzzy hug-fest at the camp. So just the fact that you were up there, and everybody is just smiling at you and being so supportive. And by the time I got done with the song it was like wheew, wow, this is cooool. So I went to camp again the next year, and when I got in the ninth grade our family moved back to Montana. And I thought my jazz career was over because I mean I went back to the sticks again.
